llm_summary: Researchers examined the bone marrow immune environment in multiple myeloma patients to understand why African Americans experience higher disease incidence, analyzing immune cell composition in 320 patients including 64 with at least 50% African genetic ancestry. Patients with high African genetic similarity showed enrichment of late-stage T cells and natural killer cells with enhanced cytotoxic capabilities, along with shifts in monocyte populations toward types associated with immune regulation and cellular cleanup rather than inflammation. The immune landscape in patients with African genetic similarity was characterized by reduced inflammatory monocytes and expanded populations of cells expressing metabolic adaptation and immunoregulatory programs. These findings suggest that African genetic ancestry is associated with a distinct bone marrow immune environment in myeloma that favors adaptive immune responses and immune regulation over innate inflammation. Further research is needed to determine whether these immune differences contribute to disease outcomes and survival in myeloma patients across different ancestry groups.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers examined the bone marrow immune microenvironment in 320 multiple myeloma patients, including 64 with ≥50% African genetic similarity (AFR-High), using immune profiling to characterize immune cell populations. AFR-High status was associated with enrichment of late T-effector cells including rare cytotoxic CD4⁺ T cells and late-differentiated adaptive NK cells expressing high cytotoxic granule proteins GNLY and GZMH. AFR-High patients demonstrated reduced CD14⁺ monocytes with expansion of CD16⁺ non-classical monocytes and macrophage-like populations enriched for metabolic adaptation, efferocytosis, and phagocytic clearance programs. These findings indicate a shift from innate inflammatory toward adaptive cytotoxic and immunoregulatory immune remodeling associated with African genetic similarity. As an observational study, these associations do not establish causal mechanisms underlying the distinct immune landscape in AFR-High patients.

title: Enriched Adaptive Immunity and Reduced Inflammatory Response in Plasma Cell Disorders of Self-Identified Black Patients.
abstract: The immune tumor microenvironment (iTME) plays a crucial role in disease biology of plasma cell (PC) dyscrasias, but remains poorly characterized in self-identified Black individuals, a population at increased risk. Mass cytometry and scRNA-seq of 128 bone marrow aspirates revealed significant changes in immune cell composition across the disease spectrum, including shifts from naïve to effector T cells with declines in B cells, MAIT, pDCs, and increases in monocytes with disease progression. Self-identified Black patients had higher relative proportions of terminally differentiated T cells and lower monocytes in newly diagnosed and treated multiple myeloma (MM). ScRNA-seq revealed genes overexpressed in self-identified Black individuals were enriched for E2F targets and G2-M checkpoints, while reduced genes were enriched for TNF-α/NF-kB, interferon and inflammatory responses pathways. These findings were supported by genetic ancestry and validated in an independent dataset of 286 patients with MM from the MMRF Immune Atlas. Self-identified race and African genetic similarity are significantly associated with remodeling the MM iTME, with potential implications for disease biology and treatment response.Copyright © 2026 American Society of Hematology.

llm_summary: Researchers examined immune cell composition in bone marrow samples from 128 patients across the plasma cell disorder disease spectrum, using advanced techniques to identify which immune cells were present and their gene expression patterns. Self-identified Black patients with multiple myeloma showed higher proportions of terminally differentiated T cells and lower monocyte levels compared to other groups, alongside distinct patterns of gene activity. Genes that were overexpressed in self-identified Black individuals were associated with cell cycle checkpoints, while underexpressed genes were linked to inflammatory pathways including TNF-α, NF-kB, and interferon responses. These findings were validated in an independent dataset of 286 multiple myeloma patients, suggesting that both self-identified race and African genetic ancestry are associated with differences in the immune tumor microenvironment. The results indicate that immune composition and inflammatory responses differ in Black patients with plasma cell disorders, which may have implications for understanding disease biology and treatment outcomes in this population at increased risk.

title: Genomic drivers of leukemia and blinatumomab response in adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia - the ECOG-ACRIN E1910 study.
abstract: The bispecific CD19/CD3 T-cell engaging antibody blinatumomab is efficacious in front-line therapy in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) but the biological determinants of response and resistance are incompletely understood. To examine the genomic determinants of outcome, we analyzed genomic and clinical data of 569 adults registered to the ECOG-ACRIN E1910 study of blinatumomab in BCR::ABL1-negative B-ALL (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02003222). We identified 23 molecular subtypes including the high-risk subtypes BCR::ABL1 (20%), BCR::ABL1-like (18%), low hypodiploid (14%) and KMT2A-R (12%), and 267 putative driver genes. We identified a subtype characterized by CEBPA overexpression or elevated CEBPB expression due to chromosomal translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking, or insertions downstream of CEBPA that generate neoenhancers. Attainment of MRD-negativity patients after induction and intensification chemotherapy was more common in PAX5alt, TCF3::PBX1 and ZNF384-R B-ALL, and less common in BCR::ABL1-like and KMT2A-R B-ALL. Integration of genomic and clinical data suggested that the addition of blinatumomab to chemotherapy was associated with improved relapse-free and overall survival for several B-ALL subtypes, including hyperdiploid, PAX5alt, PAX5 P80R, BCR::ABL1-like JAK-STAT and KMT2A-R B-ALL, although small sample sizes for several subtypes indicate that confirmation is required. Alteration of TP53 or mutations associated with myeloid clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) were identified in 15.3% and 9.8% of patients, respectively. The presence of these mutations was associated with older age at diagnosis and inferior outcome to chemotherapy. In summary, we define the landscape of genomic alterations of adult B-ALL, and identify genomic subtypes that may influence the efficacy of blinatumomab when combined with chemotherapy.Copyright © 2026 American Society of Hematology.

title: Nutraceuticals and phytoceuticals in the treatment of bipolar disorder: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract: Nutraceuticals and phytoceuticals are increasingly investigated for bipolar disorder (BD). We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, PsycINFO, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to July 1, 2025. Co-primary outcomes were changes in depressive or manic symptoms (standardized mean difference [SMD]), treatment response, and acceptability (risk ratio [RR]); tolerability and remission (RR) were secondary outcomes. Heterogeneity, transitivity, inconsistency, small-study effects, risk of bias, and confidence in evidence (CINeMA) were assessed. Twenty-eight RCTs (n=2,222) evaluated 22 treatments. No treatment outperformed placebo for depressive symptoms; placebo outperformed palmitoylethanolamide (SMD=2.69, 95% CI 1.43-3.95), based on one trial, amid substantial heterogeneity (I²=86%) but no global inconsistency. For manic symptoms, palmitoylethanolamide (SMD=-4.58, 95% CI -6.24 to -2.92) and folic acid (SMD=-2.42, 95% CI -4.06 to -0.79) outperformed placebo, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=91.3%) and no global inconsistency. Sensitivity analyses supported palmitoylethanolamide, although the finding relied on one RCT from a region producing larger-than-average SMDs. Meta-regression indicated that larger effects were associated with lower adapted AMSTAR-Plus scores. Free-and-easy-wanderer-plus™ combined with carbamazepine outperformed placebo for response and acceptability. CINeMA ratings varied and were predominantly low or very low, particularly for manic symptoms. Current evidence does not support firm recommendations for any nutraceutical or phytoceutical in acute bipolar depression or mania, and further high-quality research is needed.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. and ECNP. llm_summary: A systematic review and network meta-analysis examined whether plant-derived supplements and nutraceuticals could improve symptoms in people with bipolar disorder by analyzing 28 randomized controlled trials involving 2,222 participants that tested 22 different treatments. No nutraceutical or phytoceutical outperformed placebo for depressive symptoms, while palmitoylethanolamide and folic acid showed superiority over placebo for manic symptoms with standardized mean differences of -4.58 and -2.42 respectively, though these findings were based on limited evidence with substantial heterogeneity. A combination of free-and-easy-wanderer-plus™ with the medication carbamazepine did outperform placebo for treatment response and acceptability, representing the only intervention showing consistent benefit. title: Prognostic value of baseline modified barium swallow for perioperative dysphagia in oropharyngeal cancer: Secondary analysis of ECOG-ACRIN E3311.
abstract: Transoral surgery (TOS) for HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) demonstrated excellent oncologic outcomes, but early postoperative dysphagia remains common and clinically consequential. Identifying patients at increased risk before surgery is critical to guide early supportive care. We examined whether baseline swallowing impairment assessed by modified barium swallow (MBS) predicts early post-TOS dysphagia.In this retrospective, exploratory secondary analysis of a selected subset of Phase II ECOG-ACRIN E3311 trial, 89 patients with paired baseline and post-TOS MBS (before adjuvant therapy) underwent blinded central review using the Dynamic Imaging Grade of Swallowing Toxicity (DIGEST). The primary outcome was moderate-to-severe post-TOS dysphagia (DIGEST ≥ 2); secondary outcomes were any dysphagia (DIGEST ≥ 1) and worsening DIGEST. title: The Comorbidity-Driven Interleukin-6-Mediated Systemic Inflammation Hypothesis of Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Decade of Testing Ends in Disappointment.
abstract: In 2013, Paulus and Tschöpe proposed that the multitude of comorbidities seen in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) was causally responsible for triggering an interleukin-6 (IL-6)-mediated systemic inflammatory state that might lead to HFpEF, postulating the intermediary contribution of coronary microvascular disease and deficient nitric oxide/cyclic guanosine monophosphate (NO-cGMP) signaling and cytokine-mediated cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. The comorbidity-driven IL-6-systemic inflammation hypothesis has been extensively evaluated in randomized controlled trials. However, in these trials, most comorbidities have not been shown to represent a causal mechanism for systemic inflammation, and the treatment of comorbidities (other than obesity) has not ameliorated HFpEF. Although coronary microvascular dysfunction is common in HFpEF, it is often not endothelium-dependent, and it is not a cause of defective NO-cGMP signaling. Numerous randomized clinical trials with NO-cGMP enhancing drugs (nitrates/nitrites, phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors and soluble guanylyl cyclase stimulators) have not provided symptomatic or exercise benefits in HFpEF. Mendelian randomization studies link IL-6 to the development of HFpEF; serum levels of IL-6 precede the development and track the severity of HFpEF; and experimental models point to IL-6 as a causal mediator of HFpEF. However, the adipokine hypothesis partitioned IL-6 and other classical cytokines from pathogenic adipokines in identifying molecular mediators of HFpEF, based on the observations that systemic IL-6 does not reliably reflect visceral adipose tissue dysfunction, and it is cosecreted with neutralizing cytokine antagonists. These observations suggested systemic IL-6 represents a distal marker, and not a mediator, of adipose tissue inflammation, and thus, unlikely to play a role in HFpEF. In proteomics analyses, heightened natural endogenous cytokine antagonists are more prominent and consistent features of HFpEF than circulating levels of the cytokines themselves. The HERMES trial tested the efficacy of the IL-6 antibody, ziltivekimab, in patients with HFpEF who were enriched for cytokine-mediated systemic inflammation, but the trial has been stopped for futility. Therefore, as a result of rigorous testing of each of its mechanistic layers, it is now difficult to support the hypothesis that HFpEF is a comorbidity-driven IL-6-mediated systemic inflammatory disorder that acts through or independently of a NO-cGMP deficiency mechanism.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). title: Third Ventricular Volume as an Adjunct Imaging Marker for CSF-Venous Fistulas Causing Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension.
abstract: CSF-venous fistulas (CVFs) are an increasingly recognized cause of spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH); however, brain MRI findings may be normal in approximately 20% of patients, underscoring the need for additional imaging markers. This study aimed to evaluate third ventricular volume as an adjunct imaging biomarker for patients with CVF causing SIH, particularly in patients with low-risk conventional MRI findings.A total of 32 patients with myelographically confirmed CVF who underwent pre-treatment brain MRI were included. Third ventricular volume and total ventricular CSF volume were measured and converted to age- and sex-adjusted normative percentiles (Combinostics, Tampere, Finland). Small third ventricular volume and low total ventricular CSF volume were defined as values below the 25th normative percentile. Findings were evaluated in the overall cohort and stratified by Bern score, with low-probability Bern score defined as 0-2.The mean age was 55.7 years, and 21/32 patients were female. Mean third ventricular percentile was 21.9 ± 27.2 and mean total ventricular CSF percentile was 35.4 ± 23.7. In the overall cohort, 22/32 patients (68.8%) had small third ventricular volume, whereas 10/32 patients (31.3%) had low total ventricular CSF volume. Among patients with Bern scores of 0-2, 5/10 patients (50.0%) had small third ventricular volume, compared with 1/10 patients (10.0%) with low total ventricular CSF volume. Third ventricular percentile showed a weak to moderate positive correlation with total ventricular CSF percentile (ρ = 0.45, p = 0.0097); however, among the 22 patients with small third ventricular volume, 14 (63.6%) had preserved total ventricular CSF volume, representing 43.8% of the overall cohort (14/32). Exploratory symptom-based analyses did not identify statistically significant associations with small third ventricular volume.Reduced third ventricular volume was common in patients with CVF-related SIH and was more frequently observed than low total ventricular CSF volume, including among patients with low-probability Bern scores. title: What Is the Role of the Locus Coeruleus in Sleep, Cerebrovascular Control, and Glymphatic Clearance?
abstract: The locus coeruleus (LC) has a major role in mechanisms of arousal, attention, and emotional responses. Increasing evidence indicates that the LC also regulates sleep architecture and triggers phasic autonomic and hemodynamic events during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. Ultraslow oscillations of LC activity reduce spindle density during N2 and are phase locked to slow waves during N3, whereas LC silencing promotes the NREM-REM sleep transition. The LC also regulates the function of the neurovascular unit and promotes functional hyperemia. Recent studies show that oscillations of LC neuronal activity induce tightly synchronized cycles of vasoconstriction and vasodilation that function as a pump that propels CSF along periarterial space, thereby driving metabolite clearance via the glymphatic system. Glymphatic clearance is a fundamental mechanism for maintaining brain health and homeostasis, with broad implications for the development of preventive and therapeutic strategies in neurologic diseases.

llm_summary: The locus coeruleus, a brain region known for regulating arousal and attention, also plays an important role in controlling sleep patterns and brain blood flow. The locus coeruleus regulates the neurovascular unit and generates oscillating cycles of blood vessel constriction and dilation that function as a pump to move cerebrospinal fluid through spaces surrounding blood vessels. These fluid movements drive the glymphatic system, which is a fundamental mechanism for clearing metabolic waste products from the brain and maintaining brain health. Understanding the locus coeruleus's role in glymphatic clearance has broad implications for developing preventive and therapeutic strategies in neurologic diseases.

title: Focal Hypoganglionosis-Associated Adult-Onset Megacolon: A Localized Enteric Neuropathy Distinct From Chronic Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction.
abstract: Adult-onset megacolon is a heterogeneous disorder traditionally classified within the spectrum of idiopathic megacolon or chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction (CIPO). However, accumulating evidence suggests that a subset of patients demonstrates distinct clinicopathologic features characterized by localized motor dysfunction resulting in focal colonic narrowing, proximal megacolon, and localized hypoganglionosis. In this review, we refer to this phenotype as focal hypoganglionosis-associated adult-onset megacolon (FHAM). Clinically, patients with FHAM frequently present with severe chronic constipation, progressive abdominal distension and pain, nausea, vomiting, recurrent sub-occlusive or pseudo-obstructive episodes, and repeated decompressive interventions. Computed tomography typically demonstrates proximal megacolon with focal functional narrowing, whereas small bowel motility is preserved despite severe colonic dilatation. Histopathologic studies additionally demonstrated inflammatory ganglionitis associated with CD3-positive lymphocytic infiltration within the myenteric plexus. Molecular and physiologic studies of resected colonic tissue further revealed impaired neuromuscular signaling and smooth muscle contractility within the affected segment, suggesting localized enteric neuropathy as a potential pathogenic mechanism. Importantly, accumulating evidence suggests that patients with FHAM generally demonstrate favorable long-term outcomes following adequate surgical resection compared with patients with CIPO, including markedly lower rates of postoperative reoperation (2.5% vs. 66.7% with CIPO) and long-term total parenteral nutrition requirement (0% vs. 46.2% with CIPO). In summary, current evidence supports the concept that FHAM in adults represents a surgically remediable localized enteric neuropathic phenotype that can be clinically distinguished from classical CIPO. Recognition of this phenotype is clinically important because timely diagnosis and appropriate surgical intervention may substantially improve long-term outcomes.

title: Reproducible Amyloid Typing by Data-Independent Acquisition Mass Spectrometry.
abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS) remains underutilized in the evaluation of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue. Clinical deployment of MS in anatomic pathology is largely confined to data-dependent acquisition (DDA) work flows for amyloid typing. Alternative acquisition strategies such as data-independent acquisition (DIA) enable quantitative, peptide-centric tissue analysis and can expand MS use in biopsy evaluation.We performed DIA-based LC-MS/MS analyses of amyloid-positive tissue specimens alongside an established DDA clinical work flow. The DIA pipeline incorporated automated data processing to support standardization and transferability. Peptide peak areas were extracted using Skyline, and machine-learning classifiers and peptide scoring rules were developed to predict amyloid type.DIA peptide measurements were evaluated across 304 amyloid-positive tissue specimens representing 16 discrete amyloid types. In a development group (n = 259), a random forest classifier enabled accurate classification of the five most common amyloid types from individual LC-DIA-MS/MS injections: λ and κ immunoglobulin light chain, transthyretin, leukocyte chemotactic factor 2, and serum amyloid A. In prospective evaluation (n = 45), the combined DIA classification strategy was fully concordant with the reference DDA clinical assignments. Amyloid types not represented in classifier training were resolved using peptide-level diagnostic signals evaluated against empirically derived intensity thresholds.DIA-based mass spectrometry enables reproducible peptide-level classification of amyloid deposits in FFPE tissue. Combined with standardized data processing, machine-learning classification, and rule-based peptide scoring, this approach provides a scalable framework for proteomic amyloid typing. title: Prognostic implications of complications during VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock.
abstract: Veno-arterial extracorporeal oxygenation (VA-ECMO) provides comprehensive cardiopulmonary support in patients with cardiogenic shock (CS), but may result in complications. While complications rates are known, their impact on risk of death remains largely unknown.Using the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) Registry to identify adults with a diagnosis of CS treated with VA-ECMO (2017-2024), we analyzed the association between timing and type of complication and in-hospital mortality using three methodologies: 1) Cox proportional hazards analysis, treating complications as time-dependent covariates; 2) Multi-State Model (MSM) analysis, treating complications as transient states and estimating the differential mortality rate from each of these states; and 3) landmark Kaplan Meier survival analysis, estimating conditional survival curves, given survival to 3 weeks, based on count and timing of complications.Among 22,547 patients (31.7% female), 12,094 (54%) died during index hospitalization. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether complications occurring during veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO), a life-support technology for patients with severe heart failure, were associated with increased risk of death using data from 22,547 patients treated between 2017 and 2024. Among the cohort, 54% of patients died during hospitalization, and those who died were more likely to have experienced complications than survivors (74% versus 54%). Neurologic complications showed the strongest association with mortality risk, increasing the hazard of death by 3.6 times (95% confidence interval 3.4–3.8), while the absolute 30-day mortality risk rose from 48.6% in patients with no complications to 93.1% in those with neurologic complications. Patients who remained free of complications during the first three weeks of VA-ECMO support demonstrated the highest conditional survival rates, and the cumulative effect of multiple complications was associated with progressively greater mortality risk. These findings suggest that the occurrence and type of complications during VA-ECMO support are important markers of in-hospital mortality risk, though further research is needed.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers examined 22,547 adults with cardiogenic shock treated with veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) using the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry (2017-2024) to determine the association between complication timing and type with in-hospital mortality using Cox proportional hazards analysis, multi-state modeling, and landmark Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Among the cohort, 12,094 patients (54%) died during index hospitalization, with 74% of non-survivors experiencing complications compared to 54% of survivors. Neurologic complications increased the hazard of mortality by 3.6 (95% CI 3.4-3.8), and multi-state model analysis demonstrated that 30-day mortality risk increased from 48.6% with zero complications to 93.1% with neurologic complications. Landmark survival analysis showed that patients without complications within the first three weeks had the highest conditional survival. These findings indicate that complications on VA-ECMO have cumulative effects on mortality risk, with neurologic and pulmonary complications associated with the greatest mortality risk.

title: KDM6 Histone Demethylases Tune Pancreatic Cancer Plasticity.
abstract: Aberrant epigenetic regulation is a central driver of tumorigenesis, and the reversibility of epigenetic modifications underscores their potential as therapeutic targets. Epigenetic factors often function in a highly context-dependent manner, necessitating rigorous study of their dynamic and complex roles. Here, we uncovered an intricate regulation of tumor development and plasticity by the KDM6 family of H3K27me3 histone demethylases in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), a disease with sustained high mortality and limited treatment options. Temporally resolving KRAS-driven tumor development revealed a switch from tumor suppressive to oncogenic functions for KDM6B, with implications for tumor aggressiveness in rodents and patients. These oncogenic functions were mediated by regulation of NOTCH signaling, a pathway known to promote PDAC tumorigenesis. Concurrent elimination of KDM6A and KDM6B led to profound phenotypic changes resembling sarcomatoid carcinomas, a rare, poorly characterized subtype of human PDAC. These tumors exhibited altered oncogenic networks, including NOTCH and JNK signaling, that may support development of therapies tailored to molecular subtypes. Given the critical and distinct activities of KDM6 histone demethylases during PDAC development, targeting KDM6 activities may be beneficial in the right cellular and temporal context.

llm_summary: Epigenetic modifications that control gene expression are reversible and represent potential therapeutic targets in cancer, making it important to understand how specific epigenetic regulators function in different tumor contexts. Researchers investigated the role of KDM6 histone demethylases, which remove repressive chemical marks from DNA, in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) by studying tumor development in rodent models and analyzing patient samples. The study revealed that KDM6B switched from suppressing tumors early in development to promoting tumor aggressiveness later, with this oncogenic function operating through the NOTCH signaling pathway known to drive PDAC growth. When both KDM6A and KDM6B were eliminated together, tumors developed features resembling a rare human PDAC subtype called sarcomatoid carcinoma, with altered signaling networks including NOTCH and JNK pathways. These findings suggest that targeting KDM6 demethylases could be therapeutically beneficial, though the timing and cellular context of such interventions would be critical for effectiveness.

The study identified a functional switch in KDM6B from tumor suppressive to oncogenic activity during KRAS-driven tumorigenesis, with oncogenic functions mediated through NOTCH signaling regulation. Concurrent elimination of both KDM6A and KDM6B induced profound phenotypic changes resembling sarcomatoid carcinomas, a rare PDAC subtype, accompanied by altered NOTCH and JNK signaling networks. The findings indicate that KDM6 demethylases exhibit distinct and context-dependent activities during PDAC development. The authors note that therapeutic targeting of KDM6 activities may be beneficial only in appropriate cellular and temporal contexts, suggesting the need for molecularly tailored treatment approaches.

title: Selective Limbic and Striatal Atrophy Corresponds to Regional Gene Expression in Leucine-Rich Glioma-Inactivated-1 Immunoglobulin G Autoimmune Encephalitis.
abstract: To characterize regional brain atrophy patterns, evaluate their association with regional leucine-rich glioma-inactivated-1 (LGI1) gene expression, and identify clinical predictors of hippocampal atrophy in LGI1 autoimmune encephalitis (AE).This study compared regional brain volumes in LGI1-AE patients versus age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients. LGI1 gene expression was derived from the Allen Human Brain Atlas. Multivariable linear regression and generalized linear models were utilized.A total of 55 LGI1-AE patients were included. Median age was 68 years (IQR 62.5-74.2 years) at volumetric analysis, after 19 months (IQR 11-45 months) from symptom onset. Compared with HC (n = 55) and AD patients (n = 55), LGI1-AE patients had greater regional atrophy of the hippocampus, insula, caudate, and putamen (p < 0.002). Longitudinal analyses demonstrated hippocampal and pallidal atrophy after covariate adjustment. Among those who did not fulfill limbic encephalitis criteria and/or had non-lesional magnetic resonance imaging, limbic and striatal atrophy were identified compared with HC (p < 0.01). Regions with the greatest differential atrophy corresponded to higher LGI1 gene expression (Spearman ρ = 0.7, p = 0.005). Severe cognitive deficits at diagnosis (β = -0.56; p = 0.002) and longer disease duration (β = -0.01; p = 0.001) independently predicted total hippocampal volume (R2 = 0.31).LGI1-AE demonstrates a distinct pattern of limbic and striatal atrophy that differs from AD and aligns with regional LGI1 expression, supporting a model of selective network vulnerability. Greater baseline cognitive impairment and longer disease duration independently associated with hippocampal atrophy, underscoring the potential importance of early diagnosis and treatment to limit structural brain injury. title: Alternative lengthening of telomeres in small well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors: independent validation and cross-platform concordance.
abstract: Well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors measuring ≤ 2 cm (small PanNETs) are usually non-functional and most are discovered incidentally. While most are indolent, some behave aggressively and metastasize. Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) has shown promise as a predictive biomarker of recurrence in recent studies. We designed a multi-institutional study to validate the predictive ability of ALT in small PanNET to inform patient selection for operative versus non-operative management. We identified 172 cases of small PanNET diagnosed from 2001 to 2021 in four different institutions. ALT fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) could be performed in 133 cases and was compared with clinical outcomes. Among those with FISH, 44.4% were females with a mean age of 65.4 years (range 31-88). Twenty-one cases (15.8%) were ALT-positive. Over a median follow-up of 48 months, a total of 19 progressions (metastasis, recurrence, increase in size, or death) were recorded. ALT positivity was significantly associated with worse progression-free survival [PFS]. In the ALT-positive group, a total of 9 cases showed progression compared to 10 in the ALT-negative group (5-year PFS: 70.2% vs. 88.8%, hazard ratio: 4.69, p = 0.002). In a separate analysis using matched cases, ALT chromogenic in situ hybridization (CISH), demonstrated high concordance with ALT FISH (95.5% for positive and 91.7% for negative cases) enabling cross-platform validation. Unlike FISH, CISH can be interpreted using standard bright field microscopy, facilitating broader implementation. These findings support further evaluation of ALT testing, particularly via CISH, as a potentially scalable and accessible biomarker, while recognizing that formal analytic validation and confirmation in unselected cohorts are required before routine clinical implementation.© 2026. llm_summary: Small pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are often discovered incidentally, but some behave aggressively and metastasize, making it difficult to determine which patients need surgery versus monitoring. title: Facilitators and Barriers to Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) Electronic Patient-Reported Outcome (ePRO) Adoption in Oncology Clinical Trials: A Qualitative Study of Clinical Research Professionals (CRPs).
abstract: Interest in using patients' own mobile devices for electronic patient-reported outcome (ePRO) collection in multi-site oncology clinical trials is growing. Clinical Research Professionals (CRPs) play a key role in supporting patients' use of ePRO systems, yet their perspectives remain underexplored.To explore the facilitators and barriers to the adoption of Bring Your Own Device (BYOD)-based ePRO systems in oncology clinical trials.Twenty-three CRPs employed in institutes affiliated with National Clinical Trials Network participated in 1:1 semi-structured interviews to explore CRP perceptions of BYOD ePRO systems. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize sample characteristics and attitudes toward technology. Interview data were analyzed using content analysis.A total of 23 CRPs participated in the study. Participants were predominantly female and White, with a mean age of 40 years and an average of 7.6 years of work experience across academic and community-based sites. Interview data revealed two categories: CRP-related, which mainly addressed CRP mixed perspectives of workload change; and non-CRP-related, which addressed CRP observations of patients' poor technology competencies related to digital divide, and challenges regarding non-user-friendly system interfaces.CRP-perceived facilitators/barriers identified in this study may influence whether CRPs and clinical trial participants will embrace ePRO systems. llm_summary: Clinical Research Professionals (CRPs) play a critical role in supporting patients' use of electronic patient-reported outcome (ePRO) systems in oncology trials, yet their perspectives on adopting Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) technology—where patients use their personal mobile devices to report health information—have not been thoroughly examined. Researchers conducted semi-structured interviews with 23 CRPs employed at National Clinical Trials Network-affiliated institutes to identify facilitators and barriers to BYOD ePRO adoption in multi-site oncology clinical trials. The study found that CRPs reported mixed perspectives on how BYOD systems would change their workload, and they observed that patients often lacked the technology skills needed to use these systems effectively due to digital divides, while also noting that the system interfaces themselves were not user-friendly. These CRP-perceived facilitators and barriers may influence whether both CRPs and clinical trial participants will accept and use ePRO systems in practice. The authors conclude that additional research is needed to understand how to improve system usability for all stakeholders involved in ePRO collection.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers examined facilitators and barriers to Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) electronic patient-reported outcome (ePRO) adoption in oncology clinical trials through semi-structured interviews with 23 Clinical Research Professionals (CRPs) employed at National Clinical Trials Network-affiliated institutes. Interview data were analyzed using content analysis to identify CRP-perceived factors influencing ePRO system adoption. Two categories emerged: CRP-related factors addressing mixed perspectives on workload changes, and non-CRP-related factors including patient technology competency limitations related to digital divide and challenges with non-user-friendly system interfaces. The predominantly female and White participant sample (mean age 40 years, mean 7.6 years work experience) represented both academic and community-based sites. The study identifies CRP-perceived facilitators and barriers that may influence stakeholder adoption of ePRO systems, though additional research is needed to explore methods for improving system usability across all stakeholders.

title: Metabolic reprogramming of pathogenic CD4+ T helper cells attenuates inflammatory bowel disease in mice.
abstract: CD4+ effector T helper 1 (TH1) cells drive inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Here, we investigated how integrated signaling, metabolic, and epigenetic programs sustain their pathogenic persistence. We found that enforcing mitochondrial pyruvate metabolism with methyl pyruvate (MePyr) suppressed TH1 cell effector function and induced the acquisition of a regulatory-like phenotype. MePyr suppressed the activity of glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK3β), promoting a metabolic shift from glycolysis toward oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and limiting the accumulation of intracellular acetyl-CoA. This metabolic reprogramming decreased histone H3 acetylation at genes encoding inflammatory cytokines, thereby decreasing TH1 cell-associated gene expression. Restoration of inflammatory cytokine production by acetate supplementation or histone deacetylase inhibition established acetyl-CoA-dependent histone acetylation as a mechanistic link between metabolic flux and effector function. Conversely, the cytokine interleukin-21 enhanced TH1 cell effector activity by promoting a GSK3β-dependent shift from OXPHOS to glycolysis. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of Crohn's disease tissue revealed enrichment of glycolytic gene programs in nonregulatory CD4+ T cells. Consistent with these findings, pharmacologic inhibition of GSK3β attenuated disease severity in a T cell-transfer mouse model of colitis. Together, these findings identify a GSK3β-dependent metabolic-epigenetic axis that sustains TH1 cell pathogenicity and highlight GSK3β as a potential therapeutic target for IBD.

title: Concordance Between Area Deprivation Index and Self-Reported Income in Breast Cancer Survivors.
abstract: Self-reported income is the standard to identify low-income subjects; however, collecting this information can be onerous and subject to high levels of missing data. Area deprivation index (ADI) is a composite measure of neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage using zip code. The objective of this study was to compare the performance of ADI to self-reported income in identifying low-income individuals with breast cancer in urban and rural settings.This was a posthoc secondary analysis of women with breast cancer enrolled from 2019 to 2023 at 10 clinic sites within the National Cancer Institute Community Oncology Research program. Data were obtained from participants who self-reported income and had valid zip codes. The primary outcome was concordance between ADI and self-reported income.Among 491 patients, 190 (38.7%) reported low-income and 114 (23.2%) were identified as disadvantaged by ADI. There was fair agreement between self-reported income and ADI (k-value 0.26; 95% confidence interval, 0.17, 0.34). ADI was concordant with self-reported income for approximately two-thirds of patients. However, sensitivity in identifying low-income patients was only 37.9%. ADI sensitivity for identifying low-income patients was higher in rural than in urban settings (55% versus 33%), though agreement remained only slight (k = 0.20; 95% confidence interval, -0.005, 0.40).ADI can be a useful tool for researchers to identify low-income patients, particularly when collection of patient-level data is not feasible or missing, but limitations in sensitivity and accuracy exist.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether Area Deprivation Index (ADI), a neighborhood-based measure of socioeconomic disadvantage calculated from zip codes, could reliably identify low-income breast cancer survivors as an alternative to collecting self-reported income data. This secondary analysis included 491 breast cancer patients from 10 clinic sites who provided both self-reported income information and valid zip codes between 2019 and 2023. Among participants, 190 (38.7%) reported low income while only 114 (23.2%) were identified as disadvantaged by ADI, with fair agreement between the two measures (k-value 0.26; 95% confidence interval, 0.17, 0.34) and concordance in approximately two-thirds of patients. The ADI showed notably limited sensitivity for identifying low-income patients overall at 37.9%, though sensitivity was higher in rural settings (55%) compared to urban settings (33%). ADI may serve as a useful screening tool when direct patient data collection is infeasible or incomplete, but researchers should recognize its limitations in accurately identifying low-income individuals across different geographic settings.

Among participants, 190 (38.7%) reported low-income status while 114 (23.2%) were identified as disadvantaged by ADI, with fair agreement between the two measures (κ = 0.26; 95% confidence interval, 0.17–0.34). ADI may serve as a useful proxy for identifying low-income patients when direct data collection is infeasible or incomplete, though limitations in sensitivity and accuracy warrant consideration.

title: Sex-specific cardiovascular responses in cerulein-induced acute pancreatitis models.
abstract: Cardiovascular (CV) dysfunction is common in severe acute pancreatitis (AP) and contributes substantially to mortality. Although sex differences in CV diseases are well recognized, with males generally exhibiting higher risk and poorer outcomes, their influence on AP-associated CV responses remains poorly defined. Here, we examined sex-dependent alterations in vascular integrity and cardiac function using cerulein-induced mouse models of AP. Across both models, pancreatic injury was comparable between sexes. A modest sex difference in vascular permeability was observed in the mild but not severe AP model. In mild AP, both males and females showed similar compensatory increases in cardiac systolic function; however, in severe AP, only female mice maintained this adaptive systolic augmentation. Circulating levels of free fatty acids, reflecting systemic tissue lipolysis, were lower in females. Impaired cardiac adaptation in males was accompanied by higher levels of seven different myocardial inflammatory cytokines, as well as elevated circulating levels of angiopoietin-2 (Angpt2). While Angpt2 levels correlated with the severity of cardiac dysfunction, Angpt2 neutralization did not improve, and indeed worsened cardiac function in males. Together, these findings delineate both sex-dependent and sex-independent CV responses in mild and severe AP and identify Angpt2 as a potential compensatory cardioprotective factor under obesity-associated severe AP.

title: "I Just Want People to See Me as a Decent Human Being": Perceptions of Screening Mammography in an Underserved Group.
abstract: This qualitative study sought to understand factors related to low rates of screening mammography among transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) individuals and how these rates might be improved.Individuals who self-reported as TGD were recruited from multiple sites and national patient advocates. Consenting participants completed an individual interview using a semistructured guide informed by the Health Belief Model (HBM). Interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis.A total of 44 individuals completed the interview (median age, 44.9 years; range, 19-77 years); 11% were a racial/ethnic minority; and 52%, 20%, and 25%, respectively, self-identified as a transgender woman, transgender man, or nonbinary. Three themes emerged around constructs in the HBM. First, individuals voiced a hope to be treated equally ("I just want to go to work, pay my taxes, love my family, and go along my day and be a good human") and described how such equitable treatment during screening guarded against gender dysphoria and favored gender affirmation ("it is affirming…being treated as any other woman"). Second, barriers and facilitators related to mammography were identified, including the need to address cost/low cost ("screenings are a luxury"); prior negative/positive experiences ("they would call my name and look at me but dismiss me"); absence/presence of education ("none of the doctors…ever told me what that process looks like"); and perceived low/high cancer risk ("my mom died pretty young from breast cancer"). Finally, practical recommendations were offered, including individual changing/waiting rooms, hiring gender-diverse staff, and engaging clinicians who provide whole-person, trauma-informed care.Mammographic screening among TGD individuals could be improved by proactively creating safe, affirming spaces; working to lower costs; providing educational materials tailored to the TGD community about cancer risk and the practical aspects of screening; and hiring gender-diverse staff. These recommendations from TGD participants merit implementation as well as further study.

title: Innovations in Microsurgery: A Qualitative Appraisal of a Novel 3D-Printed Microscope.
abstract: Background Microsurgery is a critical component of plastic and reconstructive surgery. However, the high cost of training and equipment pose significant barriers, particularly in resource-limited settings. To address this challenge, the Microsurgery and Regenerative Medicine Lab within the Division of Plastic Surgery at the University of Wisconsin developed a low-cost, 3D-printed surgical microscope. This study qualitatively appraised the use of this novel microscope for microsurgery training by surveying surgeons about their experiences using this tool relative to traditional magnification methods. Methods In this prospective, multi-institutional appraisal study, surgical residents, fellows, and attending surgeons with varying microsurgical experience performed a single end-to-end microsurgical anastomosis on chicken thigh femoral arteries using the 3D-printed microscope. Participants then completed a survey assessing ease of use, adequacy for microsurgical training, educational value, and perceived impact on teaching capacity in local and global settings. Results Over 80% of participants reported that performing an end-to-end anastomosis was easier or equivalent using the 3D-printed microscope compared to surgical loupes. All respondents expressed willingness to use the device for microsurgery teaching and practice. Additionally, 91.7% (33/36) believed access to the microscope would enhance microsurgical teaching at their home institutions, and 97.1% (34/35) felt it would improve teaching capacity in globally. Qualitative feedback was overwhelmingly positive, with suggestions primarily related to ergonomics and lighting. Conclusion This study supports that this low-cost, 3D-printed microscope is an effective microsurgical training tool. Ongoing design refinements informed by user feedback may further optimize its role in expanding access to microsurgery education worldwide.Thieme. All rights reserved.

title: Central aortic pressure and LV remodeling after surgical versus transcatheter repair of coarctation of aorta: Prospective data from the MACHD-biobank.
abstract: The purpose of this study was to compare central hemodynamics, arterial function, left ventricular (LV) indices, and cardiovascular biomarkers between patients with surgical versus transcatheter coarctation of aorta (COA) repair.Prospective study of adults with repaired COA enrolled in the MACHD-Biobank Registry (2019-2024). COA patients and normal controls underwent arterial function assessment, echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and cardiovascular biomarker assay using a standardized protocol. COA patients were classified into surgical repair (COA_SR) versus transcatheter repair (COA_TR) group.We enrolled 96 COA patients (COA_SR [N = 62,65%] and COA_TR [N = 34,35%]) and 78 controls. All aortic indices, LV indices and biomarkers of fibrosis were worse in COA patients compared to controls. COA_TR group had higher aortic stiffness (aortic pulse wave velocity: 7.92 ± 1.28 versus 7.15 ± 1.34 m/s, p = 0.005), central systolic blood pressure (SBP) (119 ± 11 versus 112 ± 12 mmHg, p = 0.02), and wave reflection (augmentation index 28 ± 13 versus 22 ± 10, p = 0.009) but similar brachial SBP compared to COA_SR group. COA_TR group had higher LV mass index (85 ± 21 versus 76 ± 19 g/m2, p = 0.007), worse LV global longitudinal strain (-19 ± 3% versus -21 ± 3%, p = 0.02), and greater extracellular matrix remodeling compared to the COA_SR group. Higher aortic stiffness and wave reflection correlated with higher central SBP, while higher central SBP correlated with LV hypertrophy.Further studies are required to determine whether these observed differences central aortic hemodynamics and LV remodeling translate to differences in outcomes. title: Comparative Effectiveness of Biofeedback vs Dextranomer-Hyaluronate Injection for Fecal Incontinence: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Anal dextranomer injection and anorectal biofeedback therapy have not been rigorously compared in patients with fecal incontinence (FI) that is refractory to medical and behavioral therapy (MBT). This study compared their effectiveness, safety, and costs.The Fecal Incontinence Treatment (FIT) study was a clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03811821) conducted at 5 US medical centers. Adults with MBT-unresponsive FI (≥4 episodes/2 weeks) were randomized to receive either injections or biofeedback. The 3 outcomes were a ≥75% reduction in FI episodes at 3 months vs baseline; the proportion of patients with pelvic pain (grade ≥II), treatment-site infection, or serious adverse events (AEs) requiring hospitalization within 3 months of randomization; and treatment cost.Of 8,705 screened participants, 275 began MBT and 267 completed it. Among MBT nonresponders, 200 patients (176 [88%] women, 34 [12%] men) were randomized to injections (n=101) or biofeedback (n=99). After 3 months, FI frequency decreased by ≥75% for similar proportions of each treatment arm (injection, n=28/101 [27.7%] vs biofeedback, n=29/99 [29.3%]; adjusted odds ratio, 0.9 [95% CI, 0.5-1.7]; P=.79). Seven participants (injection, n=5; biofeedback, n=2; P=.27) had 11 relevant AEs, of which 5 were serious, non-treatment-related AEs (injection, n=3; biofeedback, n=2). Compared with biofeedback, injections cost an average of $1,563 (95% CI, $1,477-$1,649) more per patient for payers (P<.001), $38 (95% CI, -$2 to $78) more for patients (P=.06), and $1,579 (95% CI, $1,464-$1,694) more for society (P<.001).In this superiority trial, neither biofeedback nor dextranomer was superior for the primary efficacy endpoint in patients with moderate-to-severe, MBT-refractory FI. title: Clinical Implications of Hemolysis after Pulsed Field Ablation - What Can We Learn from Benchtop Models and Preclinical Experiments.
abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a transformative technology for cardiac ablation due to its efficiency and favorable safety profile. However, intravascular hemolysis has been increasingly recognized adverse effect across preclinical and clinical studies, infrequently progressing to acute kidney injury (AKI). The mechanisms, determinants, and clinical relevance of PFA-related hemolysis remain incompletely understood. Herein, we review the pathophysiology of PFA-related hemolysis and measures to mitigate its occurrence, discuss the biomarker-related changes and perform a comprehensive review of preclinical hemolysis models. Continued development of physiological benchtop models including numerical models to better understand PFA-related hemolysis and translation to bedside is needed. Furthermore, transparent cross-platform evaluation of hemolysis will be critical in the light of rapidly evolving PFA technologies.Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

title: Outcomes of Mitral Valve Intervention for Patients with Bileaflet Mitral Valve Prolapse and Preoperative Ventricular Arrhythmias.
abstract: Bileaflet mitral valve (MV) prolapse may be associated with ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Given the paucity of data analyzing the role of MV interventions, we analyzed outcomes of MV surgery in patients with bileaflet MV prolapse and preoperative ventricular arrhythmias. Between 1994 and 2018, 30 adult patients with bileaflet MV prolapse, severe MV regurgitation, and documented preoperative ventricular arrhythmias underwent MV operation at our institution. Ventricular arrhythmia was defined as ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, cardiac arrest, or bigeminy. Pre- and postoperative ventricular arrhythmias and mortality were identified from medical record review. Median age was 51 years (IQR: 41.2, 59.5), and 20 (66.7%) patients were female. The most common preoperative arrhythmia was ventricular tachycardia (73%), followed by ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. Most patients (N=28, 93.3%) underwent bileaflet MV repair, and 2 (6.7%) underwent MV replacement. There was no 30-day mortality. Ventricular arrhythmias did not recur postoperatively in 19 patients, and three patients with preoperative cardiac arrest improved without further cardiac arrest episodes but had ventricular tachycardia. The 1-year estimate of freedom from ventricular arrhythmia recurrence was 70%. Patients with recurrence were older and had longer delays between arrhythmia diagnosis and surgical referral. Higher body mass index and lower preoperative ejection fraction were associated with increased recurrence risk. In conclusion, surgical correction of bileaflet MV prolapse for severe MV regurgitation with preoperative ventricular arrhythmias can be performed safely. Although the majority of patients experienced a sustained reduction in arrhythmia burden postoperatively, recurrence was observed in a subset. Most patients (93.3%) underwent mitral valve repair, with the primary endpoint being postoperative ventricular arrhythmia recurrence. title: Self-Reported Health, Stress, and Lifestyle Behaviors Among U.S. Chief Executive Officers: A Comparison of Two Cohorts.
abstract: To evaluate self-reported health and lifestyle behaviors among U.S. Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) and to identify patterns relevant to executive healthcare delivery.An anonymous health and lifestyle survey was distributed to two populations: patients enrolled in the Mayo Clinic Executive Health Program (MC-EHP; n=14,240) and members of the Chief Executive Group (CEG; n=146,641). Data were collected between August 8 and October 2, 2025. Descriptive statistics were summarized for CEO survey responders (MC-EHP, n=792; CEG, n=613). Group comparisons were performed using Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests. No adjustment was made for multiple comparisons; therefore, inferential findings should be interpreted as exploratory.Compared with CEG CEOs, MC-EHP CEOs were older (P<.001), more likely to be male (83.5% vs 76.1%; P<.001) and White (97.0% vs 93.0%; P=.001). MC-EHP CEOs self-reported less sedentary time (6.1 vs. 6.8 hours/day; P<.001), fewer work hours (40.3 hours vs 53.8 hours/week; P<.001), and lower stress levels (4.6 vs. 6.3, P<.001). They also reported fewer sleep disturbances (P=.003), fewer chronic medical conditions and higher quality-of-life (P<.001). Use of prescription medications was higher among the MC-EHP CEOs (78.6% vs 72.0%, P=.004), whereas use of over-the-counter medications/supplements was lower (P=.022). Several statistically significant differences were modest in absolute magnitude.Among surveyed U.S. CEOs, participation in a comprehensive executive health program was associated with lower self-reported stress, healthier lifestyle behaviors, and higher quality-of-life. The findings underscore lifestyle factors relevant to overall health and highlight areas for clinicians to prioritize when treating CEO patients. Prior research suggests that CEO well-being may have broader implications for employee well-being, further supporting the need for regular patient feedback to help executive health programs adapt healthcare services to the evolving needs of their patients.Copyright © 2026. title: Radiation-Associated Lymphedema in Head and Neck Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: To estimate the pooled prevalence of lymphedema among adults with mucosal head and neck cancer treated with radiation therapy.PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Library.A comprehensive literature search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Library (2000-2025) identified cohort, case series, cross-sectional, and clinical trial studies reporting lymphedema after radiotherapy for head and neck cancer. Logit-transformed lymphedema prevalence was pooled using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman variance correction; statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using I2. This review was not prospectively registered.A total of 26 studies (n = 3133 patients) met inclusion criteria. The pooled prevalence of lymphedema was 49% (95% CI, 36%-62%), with considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 94%). Subgroup analyses yielded a pooled prevalence of 37% (12%-71%) for external and 45% (31%-60%) for internal lymphedema. Among studies reporting severity-graded data, the pooled prevalence of clinically significant (grade ≥ 2) lymphedema was 32% (14%-59%). Lymphedema definitions and assessment methods varied across the included studies, most commonly employing clinical grading. Methodological quality was mixed, reflecting the predominantly retrospective, single-arm nature of the available evidence. Overall certainty of evidence was very low. Funnel plot inspection and Egger's test suggested small-study effects (p = 0.06).Lymphedema affects nearly half of patients following radiation for head and neck cancer. These findings may support routine surveillance, early identification, and timely referral for lymphedema management within survivorship care pathways. Future prospective studies should adopt standardized definitions and outcome measures to refine risk estimates and guide prevention strategies.N/A.© 2026 The American Laryngological, Rhinological and Otological Society, Inc.

llm_summary: Researchers conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 studies involving 3,133 patients to estimate how often lymphedema develops in head and neck cancer patients treated with radiation therapy. The pooled prevalence of lymphedema was 49% (95% CI, 36%-62%), with subgroup analyses showing 37% for external lymphedema and 45% for internal lymphedema, while clinically significant cases (grade ≥ 2) occurred in 32% of patients. The considerable heterogeneity across studies (I² = 94%) and variation in how lymphedema was defined and measured across the included research suggest that these estimates should be interpreted with caution. These findings indicate that lymphedema is a common complication affecting nearly half of radiation-treated head and neck cancer survivors, which may support implementing routine surveillance and early intervention within survivorship care programs. Future prospective studies using standardized definitions and consistent outcome measures are needed to refine these prevalence estimates and better guide prevention and management strategies.

title: Amyloid PET Quantitation and Centiloid Thresholds in the Diagnosis of Alzheimer Disease: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) is increasingly used in research and clinical settings to determine the etiology of cognitive decline and eligibility for amyloid-targeting therapies. To assist with amyloid PET evaluation and to guide clinical decision-making, images can be quantified in a standardized unit called Centiloid, the interpretation of which can vary according to the method and threshold used.To collect Centiloid values from available studies and determine robust positivity cutoffs using data-driven methods and correspondence with visual reads.PubMed search (October 2024) identified studies with Centiloid values. Corresponding authors were invited to share individual participant data. Additional data were obtained through access-controlled repositories and conference outreach (July 2024-July 2025).Studies were included if they provided Centiloids, radiotracer, age, and sex.Each study was analyzed using a unified statistical pipeline; study estimates were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis.Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) were fitted to Centiloid values for each study. In studies with a bimodal distribution (per integrated completed likelihood), single cutoffs for positivity were set as mean plus 2 SDs of the lower gaussian component. Using GMMs, a double-cutoff approach defined a lower certainty range using a 90% posterior probability cutoff for assignment to the low (amyloid-negative) vs high (amyloid-positive) component. An alternative Centiloid cutoff was derived from maximizing the correspondence (Cohen κ) with the binary visual reads when available.This meta-analysis included cross-sectional amyloid PET scans acquired with 5 radiotracers from 49 227 participants across 53 studies from 15 countries (mean age, 71 years; 54% female, 62% cognitively impaired). The data-driven GMM approach identified a bimodal distribution in 51 studies (n = 48 786), resulting in a single cutoff for positivity of 18 Centiloids (95% CI,16-19; I2 = 97%). The double-cutoff approach revealed high confidence for interpreting scans as negative when Centiloid values were lower than 11 (95% CI, 9-13; I2 = 95%) and interpreting scans as positive if Centiloid values were higher than 26 (95% CI, 24-28; I2 = 95%). In analyses of correspondence with binary (positive or negative) visual reads of amyloid PET scans (n = 35 045; 36 studies), Centiloids were highly predictive of visual positivity (Cohen κ, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.83-0.89; I2 = 96%) with a cutoff of 27 Centiloids (95% CI, 24-30; I2 = 80%).In this individual participant data meta-analysis, positivity cutoffs converged around 18 Centiloids (data-driven) and 27 Centiloids (visual reads). Findings from a double-cutoff analysis suggest that scans in the 11 to 26 Centiloid range should be interpreted with caution depending on the context of use.

llm_summary: Researchers examined amyloid PET imaging data from 49,227 participants across 53 studies to establish standardized cutoff values for determining whether patients have amyloid accumulation in the brain, which is relevant for diagnosing Alzheimer disease and determining eligibility for new treatments. Using statistical methods to analyze the distribution of Centiloid values (a standardized measurement unit for amyloid PET scans) across five different radiotracers, the study identified a single positivity cutoff of 18 Centiloids through data-driven analysis and a cutoff of 27 Centiloids when comparing to visual interpretation by experts. A double-cutoff approach revealed that scans with values below 11 Centiloids could be confidently interpreted as negative for amyloid, while values above 26 Centiloids could be confidently interpreted as positive, with strong agreement between Centiloid measurements and visual reads (Cohen κ = 0.86). The convergence of cutoff values around 18 to 27 Centiloids across different analytical approaches provides clinicians with evidence-based thresholds for amyloid P.
llm_summary_expert: This individual participant data meta-analysis pooled Centiloid values from amyloid PET scans acquired with 5 radiotracers across 49,227 participants from 53 studies to establish standardized positivity cutoffs for Alzheimer disease diagnosis. Gaussian mixture models identified bimodal distributions in 51 studies (n=48,786), yielding a single positivity cutoff of 18 Centiloids (95% CI, 16-19). A double-cutoff approach defined high confidence for negative scans below 11 Centiloids (95% CI, 9-13) and positive scans above 26 Centiloids (95% CI, 24-28), while correspondence analysis with binary visual reads (n=35,045) identified a cutoff of 27 Centiloids (95% CI, 24-30; Cohen κ=0.86). Scans in the 11 to 26 Centiloid range demonstrated substantial heterogeneity across studies (I²=95-97%) and should be interpreted cautiously depending on clinical context.

title: Comparative Effectiveness of Treatments for Relapse Prevention in Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibody-Associated Disease.
abstract: The most effective treatment strategy to prevent relapses after a first myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) event remains unclear. Our objective was to evaluate the comparative effectiveness of maintenance therapies in preventing relapses in pediatric-onset MOGAD.We analyzed prospectively collected data from November 2011 to August 2023 across 13 US pediatric neuroimmunology centers. Eligible patients had demyelinating disease onset before age 18 years, confirmed MOG-IgG positivity through cell-based assay, and negative aquaporin-4 IgG. Maintenance therapies were defined as ≥90 consecutive days of treatment and included IV immunoglobulin (IVIG), anti-CD20 therapy, oral corticosteroids, and other immunosuppressants. Two complementary approaches were used: (1) a primary full-course analysis using time-varying Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for a priori-selected confounders, accounting for treatment changes throughout the disease course, and (2) a secondary early-course analysis using 1:1 propensity score-matched Cox models for the first qualifying treatment initiated within 90 days of onset, applying an intention-to-treat framework to minimize immortal time bias.Among 312 patients (58% female; mean age at onset 8.9 ± 4.2 years), 145 (46%) experienced at least 1 relapse during a median follow-up of 2.53 years (interquartile range 0.75-5.26). In the full-course analysis, IVIG was associated with a statistically significant 46% reduction in relapse risk (hazard ratio [HR] 0.54; 95% CI 0.31-0.93; p = 0.028). Anti-CD20 therapy (HR 0.98; 95% CI 0.56-1.72), oral corticosteroids (HR 0.86; 95% CI 0.55-1.35), and other immunosuppressants showed no significant association with relapse risk. In the early-course propensity-matched analysis, directional trends favoring IVIG (n = 23 matched pairs; HR 0.29; 95% CI 0.07-1.14; p = 0.076) and anti-CD20 therapy (n = 6 matched pairs; HR 0.34; 95% CI 0.03-3.82; p = 0.38) were observed but did not reach statistical significance, likely due to limited sample sizes. Oral corticosteroids showed a nonsignificant trend toward increased relapse risk in early-course analysis (HR 2.18; 95% CI 0.79-6.31; p = 0.13). Older age at disease onset independently increased relapse hazard (HR 1.67 per year; 95% CI 1.49-1.87; p < 0.001), and prior relapse count was a strong predictor of future relapse risk.In this large, prospective, multicenter pediatric MOGAD cohort, IVIG was the only treatment consistently associated with reduced relapse risk across both analytical approaches, supporting its potential role as first-line maintenance therapy. Anti-CD20 therapy showed directional trends warranting further investigation. Key limitations include potential residual confounding by indication and small sample sizes in certain treatment categories. Randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings.

title: National Delphi Study to Inform Modernization of Anesthesiology Residency Case Log Requirements.
abstract: The Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME; Chicago, Illinois) case log system establishes minimum clinical experiences for anesthesiology residency. While core program requirements were last updated in 2016, case log minimums themselves have not undergone a major revision in approximately 2 decades. Consequently, current requirements may not fully reflect changes in anesthetic practice and the evolving scope of perioperative medicine. In anticipation of major ACGME revisions in 2027, this study aimed to develop consensus-driven recommendations for modernizing residency case logs.A three-round modified Delphi study was conducted with a nationally representative panel of 60 stakeholders, including anesthesiology residency program directors and academic and private practice anesthesiologists. Panelists evaluated a comprehensive list of potential case categories across three domains: technical skills, surgical case characteristics, and patient demographics. In round 1, panelists proposed minimum numbers or suggested that no requirement was necessary. Rounds 2 and 3 utilized iterative feedback to determine consensus on the necessity of requirements and specific minimum thresholds. Consensus was defined as at least two-thirds agreement.Sixty invited experts completed all three rounds (100% response rate). The panel reached consensus to recommend new minimum requirements across several areas not currently tracked with minimums, including arterial lines (40), central lines (20), fiberoptic intubation (10), one-lung ventilation (10), neuromonitoring (10), point-of-care ultrasound (10 cardiac, 10 lung), and non-operating room anesthesia (20 cases). Regarding existing requirements, consensus was reached to recommend increasing total peripheral nerve blocks from 40 to 60, with added requirements for anatomic specificity, and cardiac case minimums from 20 to 25. The panel also established consensus definitions for life-threatening pathologies to standardize reporting. The panel did not achieve consensus on several areas, including, for example, whether a minimum requirement for patients younger than 3 months should be maintained.These findings provide stakeholder-validated recommendations to inform upcoming ACGME requirement revisions.Copyright © 2026 American Society of Anesthesiologists. title: Clinical and genetic characterization of FUS-associated ALS in a tertiary cohort.
abstract: An understanding of FUS-related ALS is becoming increasingly actionable with the emergence of targeted therapies. We retrospectively reviewed patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and reported FUS variants evaluated across all Mayo Clinic sites between January 2009 and June 2026. Variants were reevaluated according to ACMG/AMP criteria, and clinical and genetic data were abstracted from medical records. The primary cohort included 12 unrelated patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) FUS variants; 6 patients with variants of uncertain significance were retained descriptively. Pathogenic variants clustered in the C-terminal region, including one previously unreported likely pathogenic frameshift variant, c.1491_1494dup. Patients with pathogenic variants showed early-onset, rapidly progressive disease with frequent bulbar or respiratory onset, predominant lower motor neuron findings, and short survival. Observed phenotypes were broadly consistent with previous variant-specific reports. These findings expand variant-specific natural history data in FUS-ALS and may inform prognosis, patient stratification, and the interpretation of emerging FUS-targeted therapeutic studies.

title: Accuracy of Plasma Cell-Free DNA Polymerase Chain Reaction for Diagnosis of Coccidioidomycosis.
abstract: Coccidioidomycosis is the most prevalent endemic mycosis in the United States. Diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis can be challenging due to limitations of conventional diagnostics. Detection of fungal plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is a novel noninvasive testing modality for the diagnosis of invasive fungal disease. In this study, we characterized the performance of Coccidioides plasma cfDNA polymerase chain reaction (PCR).A retrospective study was conducted in patients with suspected coccidioidomycosis who underwent plasma cfDNA PCR testing and conventional fungal testing for Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii. Patients were categorized per the EORTC/MSGERC case definitions as proven or probable for sensitivity analyses and no coccidioidomycosis for specificity analyses.Overall, 362 plasma samples from unique patients were included in this study. The overall sensitivity, specificity, and positive- and negative-predictive values of Coccidioides plasma cfDNA PCR at 0.04% prevalence were 57.5% (27/47; 95% CI, 42.2%-71.7%), 100% (315/315; 95% CI, 98.8%-100%), 100% (95% CI, 87.2%-100%), and 100% (95% CI, 100%-100%), respectively. The sensitivity was 33.3% (2/6; 95% CI, 4.3%-77.7%) in patients with pulmonary focal disease, 66.7% (14/21; 95% CI, 43.0%-85.4%; P≥.05) in patients with pulmonary multifocal disease, and 52.6% (10/19; 95% CI, 39.6%-77.9%; P≥.05) in patients with disseminated coccidioidomycosis. In patients with concurrent antigen results, the sensitivity of cfDNA PCR was 58.3% (14/24; 95% CI, 39.6%-77.9%) compared with 37.5% (9/24; 95% CI, 18.8%-59.4%; P≥.05) for antigen.Coccidioides plasma cfDNA PCR is modestly sensitive but highly specific, which can be useful for rapid and noninvasive diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis.© The Author(s) 2026. title: Prevalence and Outcomes of Bacterial Co-detections by Blood Culture Among Children and Adults Hospitalized With Laboratory-confirmed Influenza, Influenza Hospitalization Surveillance Network, 2022-2024.
abstract: Influenza predisposes individuals to bacterial co-infections, which can result in disseminated infection and bacteremia. We describe the epidemiology and outcomes of blood culture co-detections among those hospitalized with influenza over 2 influenza seasons.We sampled individuals of all ages from FluSurv-NET, a US population-based surveillance network of persons hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed influenza, during the 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 seasons. Surveillance staff collected information on bacterial blood cultures within 3 days before or 3 days following admission. We described patient characteristics and in-hospital outcomes, stratified by culture positivity, number of positive cultures, and type of co-detection, using unweighted counts and weighted percentages to account for the complex survey design.Overall, 14 316 patients were included, with a median (interquartile range) age of 57 (14-74) years, 53.6% female, 52.0% non-Hispanic White, and 25.6% with ≥4 categories of underlying medical conditions. Of these, 50.8% had ≥1 blood cultures obtained and 5.2% overall had ≥1 bacterial co-detections. Intensive care unit admission occurred for 9.6%, 19.2%, 31.2%, and 47.9% among patients with no blood cultures, negative cultures, 1 co-detection, and >1 co-detection documented, respectively; in-hospital mortality occurred in 1.5%, 3.3%, 9.4%, and 14.5%, respectively. Among patients with positive cultures, 22.1% had Staphylococcus aureus and 7.5% had Streptococcus pneumoniae co-detections; both were associated with severe illness (with 22.4% in-hospital mortality each).Bacterial co-detections in persons hospitalized with influenza were associated with poor in-hospital outcomes. Efforts to prevent severe influenza and bacterial co-infections, including through vaccination, may reduce substantial morbidity and mortality from influenza.Published by Oxford University Press on behalf of Infectious Diseases Society of America 2026.

llm_summary: Researchers examined bacterial co-infections in hospitalized patients with influenza because these secondary infections can lead to severe complications and death. The study analyzed 14,316 patients from a US surveillance network during the 2022-2024 influenza seasons, collecting information on bacterial blood cultures obtained within three days before or after hospital admission. Among all patients, 5.2% had at least one bacterial co-detection, and those with co-detections experienced substantially worse outcomes, including in-hospital mortality rates of 9.4% with one co-detection and 14.5% with multiple co-detections compared to 3.3% among those with negative cultures. Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae were the most common co-detected bacteria, each associated with 22.4% in-hospital mortality. These findings suggest that preventing severe influenza and bacterial co-infections through measures such as vaccination could reduce significant illness and death in hospitalized patients.

Blood cultures were obtained in 50.8% of patients, with 5.2% overall demonstrating ≥1 bacterial co-detections; intensive care unit admission rates were 9.6%, 19.2%, 31.2%, and 47.9% for patients with no cultures, negative cultures, 1 co-detection, and >1 co-detection, respectively, while in-hospital mortality rates were 1.5%, 3.3%, 9.4%, and 14.5%. Among culture-positive patients, Staphylococcus aureus (22.1%) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (7.5%) were the most common co-detections, each associated with 22.4% in-hospital mortality. title: EACTS Expert Consensus Document on aortic valve repair and valve-sparing aortic root replacement procedures.
abstract: Aortic valve repair is a complex and evolving field that requires multidisciplinary teamwork among heart specialists to diagnose and treat various causes and mechanisms of aortic regurgitation and proximal thoracic aortic aneurysms across all age groups. From a surgical standpoint, aortic valve repair includes all procedures aimed at restoring or maintaining native valve function. This European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) Expert Consensus Document critically evaluates the current evidence on the common causes and mechanisms of aortic regurgitation, the use of echocardiographic parameters in patient selection, intraoperative assessment, and prognostic evaluation as well as the surgical techniques in practice. It outlines fundamental surgical principles shared across different repair methods and provides consensus statements to guide clinical practice. These statements are intended for a broad audience, including paediatric and adult cardiologists, echocardiographers, cardiovascular imaging specialists, and cardiac surgeons. Where high-quality evidence is unavailable, the guidance relies on the collective experience and expert judgement of the multidisciplinary author team.
